notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes for **1 Samuel 17:30–58**, drawn from the sources accessed.

---

## v. 30 — David turns to another and asks again

- **David persisted despite his brother’s rebuke.** After Eliab’s angry accusation, David turned to another soldier and repeated his questions about the reward and about the uncircumcised Philistine defying the armies of the living God. The people gave him the same answer as before. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/17-30.htm — Gill)
- **David was “secretly moved by God’s Spirit”** to undertake the combat. By speaking to multiple people, his words would spread and eventually reach Saul’s ears — David in modesty did not go directly to the king. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/17-30.htm — Benson / Pulpit)
- **Keil & Delitzsch note:** David answered Eliab “very modestly … ‘What have I done, then? It was only a word’” — then turned to another and repeated himself. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/17-30.htm — K&D)
- **Matthew Henry observes:** David’s conquest of his own passion under Eliab’s provocation “was more honourable than that of Goliath.” He did not render railing for railing but gave a soft answer. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/17-30.htm — MHC)

---

## v. 31 — David’s words reported to Saul; Saul sends for him

- **David’s words were overheard and reported.** His bold, indignant tone — so unlike the fear of everyone else — attracted attention. The bystanders “rehearsed his words to Saul, and Saul sent for him.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/1-samuel-17.html — Expositor’s Bible Commentary)
- **Matthew Henry:** “A little shepherd, come but this morning from keeping sheep, has more courage than all the mighty men of Israel, and encourages them.” God often sends good words to His Israel and does great things through “the weak and foolish things of the world.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/17-32.html — MHC)

---

## v. 32 — David volunteers: “Let no man’s heart fail … your servant will go and fight”

- **This is the first time David specifically volunteers** to fight Goliath. Before this, he only asked why someone didn’t fight. Now he says, “*I* will.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/ — Guzik)
- **David says nothing about the reward.** He does not mention riches, the king’s daughter, or tax exemption. His concern is for the honour of God and Israel, not personal gain. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/17-32.html — MHC)
- **Guzik (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** David’s words almost sounded like youthful overconfidence — “Let no man’s heart fail” coming from a teenage boy. But it was not pride; it was faith. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)

---

## v. 33 — Saul’s objection: “You are just a boy”

- **Saul saw only outward appearances.** He measured by “a carnal standard” — David was a youth, Goliath had been a warrior from his youth. Saul could not see the spiritual dimension. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/1-samuel-17.html — Expositor’s Bible Commentary)
- **Guzik:** Saul looked at the “tale of the tape” in natural terms and thought David was disqualified by age, size, and inexperience. “The outward ‘tale of the tape’ said there was no way David could win. The ‘tale of God’s tape’ said there was no way David could lose.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)

---

## v. 34–36 — David recounts killing the lion and the bear

- **David’s shepherd years were God’s training ground.** As a shepherd tending his father’s sheep, he had fought and killed both a lion and a bear that attacked the flock. God prepared David for Goliath through his daily faithfulness. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)
- **“This uncircumcised Philistine will be like one of them.”** David equates Goliath with the wild beasts because Goliath has defied “the armies of the living God” — the same God David served as a shepherd. David’s boldness grows: first he said someone should fight (v.26), then *he* would fight (v.32), now he says he will *kill* Goliath. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)
- **The “beard” or “fur” (v.35):** Gill notes that “his beard” is put for the throat or under-jaw, since neither lion nor bear has a beard properly speaking. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/17-37.htm — Gill)

---

## v. 37 — “The LORD who delivered me … will deliver me”

- **David’s faith rested on past deliverance as a pledge of future deliverance.** He did not boast in his own prowess but ascribed his victories over the lion and bear entirely to the Lord. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/17-37.htm — JFB)
- **Matthew Henry:** If God helped David rescue a single lamb, would He not help him rescue a whole nation? The remembrance of God’s past deliverance “confirmed his faith and urged him to the conflict.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/1-samuel-17.html — Expositor’s Bible Commentary)
- **Saul’s reply: “Go, and may the LORD be with you.”** The Pulpit Commentary notes that Saul’s pious language recalls the Saul of old, before the Spirit departed from him. It was a courageous act of trust for Saul, since the fate of the nation hung on this single combat. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/17-37.htm — Pulpit)
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** The Targum renders Saul’s blessing as “the Word of the Lord be for thy help.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/17-37.htm — K&D)

---

## v. 38–39 — Saul clothes David in his armour; David rejects it

- **Saul was still thinking in the natural.** He assumed David needed the best human armour available — the king’s own. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)
- **David could not walk in Saul’s armour** because (a) it did not physically fit — everything was too big; (b) it did not spiritually fit — human armour, military technology, or worldly wisdom would not win this battle; the LORD would. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)
- **Guzik on application:** “David had to renounce Saul’s armor. He had to vow, ‘I will not fight with man’s armor. I will trust in the LORD and His armor instead.’ Often, we want a safe ‘middle ground’ where we try to wear both kinds of armor. God wants us to trust in Him and Him alone.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)
- **Trapp (quoted by Guzik):** Some Christians must say the same about the armour of God: “I cannot do withal, for I have not been accustomed to it.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)

---

## v. 40 — David takes his staff, five smooth stones, and his sling

- **“It was a true stroke of military genius”** — Ellicott says David determined to fight only with weapons he knew and in which he was highly skilled. “He was like one armed with a rifle, while his enemy had only a spear and a sword.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/17-40.htm — Ellicott)
- **David used the same tools God had used before** — the staff, sling, and shepherd’s bag — to kill the lion and the bear. What God used before, He would use again. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)
- **Why five stones?** Several views appear:
  - **Practical reserve:** David chose five in case the first shot missed (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-17.html — Constable)
  - **Goliath’s relatives:** A rabbinic and popular suggestion — though not in the text — is that Goliath had four giant relatives (see 2 Samuel 21:18–22) and David prepared for them too. Guzik calls this “charming – but purely legendary.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)
  - **Smooth stones** were chosen because they would fly more freely from the sling with greater force and accuracy. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-samuel-17.html — Clarke)
- **Augustine’s allegorical reading (quoted by Ellicott/Wordsworth):** The five smooth stones represent the five books of Moses. Christ, the greater David, took “what was solid out of what was fluid … what was moral and perpetual out of what was ceremonial and temporary” — and with one stone (a text from Deuteronomy) He overthrew Satan at the temptation. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/17-40.htm — Ellicott citing Augustine, Sermon 32)

---

## v. 41–42 — Goliath advances with his shield-bearer; he despises David

- **Goliath’s shield-bearer went before him**, likely carrying a large shield, because Goliath’s own hands were full with sword and spear. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_samuel/17.htm — Matthew Henry)
- **Goliath “despised him”** — he looked for a tall, strong warrior and instead saw a boy, “ruddy and handsome,” who looked fitter for dancing than for battle. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_samuel/17.htm — MHC)

---

## v. 43–44 — “Am I a dog?” Goliath curses and threatens David

- **“Am I a dog, that you come at me with sticks?”** David’s shepherd’s staff looked contemptible to the heavily armed giant. Goliath saw only the outward — a boy with sticks. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_samuel/17.htm — MHC)
- **Goliath cursed David by his gods** — invoking the impotent vengeance of Philistine idols (such as Dagon). He thought this would guarantee his success. Matthew Henry calls this “the security and presumption of fools.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_samuel/17.htm — MHC)
- **Goliath’s threat (v.44):** “I will give your flesh to the birds” — he spoke with absolute confidence, but his confidence was in himself, not in God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)

---

## v. 45–47 — David’s speech: “I come to you in the name of the LORD of Hosts”

- **David contrasts weapons:** “You come against me with sword and spear and javelin, but I come against you in the name of the LORD of Hosts.” Goliath trusted in military hardware; David trusted in the God whom Goliath had defied. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)
- **Matthew Henry:** David’s speech “savours nothing of ostentation, but God is all in all in it.” He derives his authority from God, depends for success upon God, and devotes all glory to God. David approaches the combat “rather as a priest that was going to offer a sacrifice to the justice of God than as a soldier.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_samuel/17.htm — MHC)
- **David’s two purposes (vv.46–47):**
  1. **“Then the whole world will know that there is a God in Israel”** — a missionary, worldwide purpose. The God of Israel is the one true God.
  2. **“All those assembled here will know that it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves”** — a lesson for Israel itself: deliverance comes from God, not military might. “The battle is the LORD’s.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)
- **“LORD of Hosts”** (YHWH Sabaoth) means the LORD of armies — David acknowledges God as the true Commander of Israel’s forces. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)

---

## v. 48–49 — David runs toward Goliath; the stone sinks into his forehead

- **David “ran quickly toward the battle line.”** He did not retreat or freeze. Guzik: “Trusting God and working hard are not opposites but go together.” David showed active faith — sprinting toward the enemy while relying completely on God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)
- **The stone struck Goliath’s forehead and “sank into” it.** Matthew Henry: Goliath apparently went with his helmet’s face-guard (beaver) open, and God’s providence directed the stone to the one exposed spot. One rabbinic tradition holds that when Goliath threw his head back to taunt David, his helmet fell off. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_samuel/17.htm — MHC)
- **Goliath “fell facedown.”** Guzik notes the parallel: just as the Philistine god Dagon fell facedown before the ark of the LORD (1 Samuel 5:3–4), so Goliath fell facedown before the LORD’s anointed. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)
- **Matthew Henry:** “See how frail and uncertain life is, even when it thinks itself best fortified, and how quickly, how easily, and with how small a matter, the passage may be opened for life to go out and death to enter.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_samuel/17.htm — MHC)

---

## v. 50–51 — David prevails without a sword; he beheads Goliath

- **“Without a sword in his hand he struck down the Philistine and killed him.”** The text emphasises this — it was not by conventional military means that David won. Then he used Goliath’s own sword to cut off his head. Matthew Henry: “God is greatly glorified when his proud enemies are cut off with their own sword.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_samuel/17.htm — MHC)
- **David’s victory is a type of Christ’s victory** over Satan — “whom he spoiled, and made a show of them openly (Colossians 2:15), and we through him are more than conquerors.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_samuel/17.htm — MHC)
- **The Philistines fled when they saw their champion dead.** Their entire strategy depended on Goliath. Once he fell, they had no confidence left. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)

---

## v. 52–53 — Israel pursues the Philistines and plunders their camp

- **The men of Israel and Judah “charged forward with a shout.”** The same army that had been paralyzed with fear for forty days now pursued the Philistines all the way to Gath and Ekron. The death of one man reversed the morale of two armies. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)
- **The Philistine dead were strewn along the Shaaraim road.** This detail underscores the totality of the rout — the Philistines were cut down as they fled. (https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/1_samuel/17.htm)
- **Israel plundered the Philistine camp** — what belonged to the enemy now enriched God’s people. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_samuel/17.htm — MHC)

---

## v. 54 — David brings Goliath’s head to Jerusalem; keeps the weapons

- **David brought the head to Jerusalem.** Matthew Henry says this served as “a terror to the Jebusites” who still held the stronghold of Zion at that time — a preview that Jerusalem would one day be David’s city. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_samuel/17.htm — MHC)
- **Goliath’s weapons were placed in David’s own tent**, except the sword, which was later kept “behind the ephod in the tabernacle” as consecrated to God (1 Samuel 21:9). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_samuel/17.htm — MHC)

---

## v. 55–58 — Saul asks, “Whose son is this young man?”

- **The apparent contradiction:** In 1 Samuel 16:18–23, David had already served at Saul’s court as a musician and armour-bearer. How could Saul now not know who David was? This is a well-known difficulty that commentators address in several ways. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/17-55.htm — Ellicott)
- **Explanation 1 — Saul asked about lineage, not identity.** He knew David’s person but needed to know his father’s name and family background, since he had promised the victor’s father’s house would be made “free in Israel” (v.25) and his daughter in marriage. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/17-55.htm — Ellicott, Benson; also Keil & Delitzsch: the question “does not presuppose an actual want of acquaintance with the person of David … but only ignorance of the social condition of David’s family.”)
- **Explanation 2 — Saul’s mental illness caused forgetfulness.** Saul’s distressing spirit (1 Samuel 16:14) may have affected his memory. Coupled with the passage of time and David’s changed appearance (he had grown, was now in shepherd’s dress rather than courtly attire), Saul simply did not recognise him. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/17-55.htm — Gill, JFB, Poole)
- **Explanation 3 — Chronological rearrangement.** Some hold that the events of chapter 17 occurred before chapter 16 chronologically, though the compiler placed them in this order for thematic reasons. Constable: “the text is not focused on chronological reporting but intends rather a dual topical introduction of David.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/17-55.html — Constable, citing Longman & Dillard)
- **Explanation 4 — The LXX simply omitted the difficult verses.** The Septuagint (Greek OT) cuts verses 12–31 and 55–58, plus 18:1–5, to remove the inconsistency. Modern scholars generally see this as an attempt to solve a problem rather than reflecting the original text. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/17-55.htm — Ellicott; Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges notes that vv.55–58 are not found in LXX [B])
- **Explanation 5 — Saul dissembled.** Knowing the rumour of Samuel anointing a new king, and now seeing David’s triumph, Saul may have pretended not to know him “with a view to accomplish the destruction of this young and formidable rival.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/17-55.html — Lange, cited on StudyLight)
- **David’s answer (v.58):** “I am the son of your servant Jesse of Bethlehem.” David answers modestly and truthfully. He does not boast about his victory but simply identifies his father. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/17-58.htm — Gill)
- **Guzik:** David’s self-identification as “the son of your servant Jesse the Bethlehemite” is humble and straightforward. From this point, David “was introduced to the court with much greater advantages than before.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)

---

## Denominational and Other Distinctives

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word – David Guzik):**
- Emphasis on the Holy Spirit’s role throughout: David’s victory was won *in his heart* before the stone was ever slung, when he refused to let Eliab’s harsh words knock him off course. “If Eliab’s hurtful words could get David in the flesh and out of step with the Spirit of the LORD, then David’s strength would be gone.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)
- David’s running toward Goliath is held up as a model of active faith: trusting God *and* working hard together — not passive waiting. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/)

**Reformed / Traditional Protestant (Matthew Henry, JFB, Keil & Delitzsch):**
- Matthew Henry stresses God’s sovereignty: the stone was guided not so much by David’s skill as by “God’s providence.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_samuel/17.htm — MHC)
- The typological reading — David as a type of Christ defeating Satan — is prominent. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_samuel/17.htm — MHC)

**Baptist (Spurgeon, cited in Guzik/Enduring Word):**
- Spurgeon is quoted saying: “Immediately before the encounter with the Philistine he fought a battle which cost him far more thought, prudence, and patience. The word-battle in which he had to engage with his brothers and with king Saul, was a more trying ordeal to him than going forth in the strength of the Lord to smite the uncircumcised boaster.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/, citing Spurgeon)

**Catholic / Patristic (Augustine, via Ellicott/Wordsworth):**
- Augustine saw the five smooth stones as the five books of Moses (the Pentateuch). Christ took these “stones” out of the flowing stream of Judaism — taking what was solid and permanent — and with one stone (a text from Deuteronomy) He overthrew Satan in the temptation. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/17-40.htm — Ellicott, quoting Augustine’s Sermon 32)

**Modern Scholarship (text-critical):**
- The Septuagint (LXX) omits vv.12–31 and 55–58, suggesting these sections may have been absent from the Greek translator’s Hebrew text or were deliberately excised to remove the apparent contradiction about Saul not knowing David. Most conservative commentators (Keil, Ellicott) argue the Hebrew text is original and offer harmonising explanations. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/17-55.htm — Ellicott; Cambridge)
- Goliath’s height: The Masoretic Hebrew text reads “six cubits and a span” (about 9′9″). However, the LXX, Josephus, and a Qumran manuscript (4QSama) read “four cubits and a span” (about 6′9″). Modern translations are divided (e.g., NRSV, ESV follow the Hebrew; NAB follows the shorter reading). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-17-commentary — NET Note)
